cards.title: Diagnose Shopify's Composite Speed Score
cards.summary: Shopify's admin speed score averages home, collection and product page timings — not a single URL test.
cards.use_when: You need to make sense of the speed score in your Shopify admin versus a single-page Google/Lighthouse test, or you want to know which templates to optimize when improving store speed.
steps: Open the speed score in the Shopify admin and click through to see which pages Shopify says it measures — typically the home page, a collection page and a product page (the most-trafficked ones).
Test those pages yourself multiple times (the source suggests running each 3–4 times and averaging) because a single run varies widely; the Shopify score is essentially an average of the three pages.

Recognize that if you have multiple product or collection templates, fixing only the template Shopify links to gives partial improvement; editing all templates for a page type produces extra speed gain.
After fixing images, scripts or assets, expect a delay before the dashboard score updates — the source's experience is roughly 12–24 hours, driven by store traffic rather than an instant refresh.
Combine the Shopify score with Google PageSpeed Insights and Chrome Lighthouse, since Google surfaces only the top issues and others appear as you fix them.
caveats: Score refresh timing (12–24h) is the presenter's field observation, not a documented SLA; verify against current Shopify reporting.

cards.title: Set a CLS Target and Find Shifts in Lighthouse Trace
cards.summary: Fix layout shift by reserving space for late-loading header, widget and thumbnail elements identified in a Lighthouse 'original trace' inspection.
cards.use_when: Google Search Console flags CLS, a store's organic ranking drops, or you need to find which above-the-fold elements move during page load on your home or product pages.
steps: Run a Lighthouse test in Chrome, then choose 'View Original Trace' and watch the timeline: note the first paint and each point where new elements appear and push existing content down.

In the source's example cases, the culprits were the top menu/header appearing late, the Afterpay widget injecting and pushing content down, and product thumbnails appearing at the bottom — all above the fold.
For an element whose size is contradicted by two CSS rules (e.g. two stylesheets setting different heights), remove one conflicting rule.

For an app that injects a widget (like reviews), determine the container size the widget needs and add CSS reserving that fixed width and height so the rest of the page doesn't move when the widget loads.
Repeat across home, collection and product pages, since each has different apps and scripts loading.
caveats: The source's target: keep CLS under 0.25, ideally near 0.1 or 0; the presenter's case dropped 0.73 → 0.13 → 0.1 → 0 over roughly 28 days, which is an example, not a promise.
CLS data in Search Console lags real fixes by days/weeks.

cards.title: Recompile Critical CSS for Lazy-Loaded Theme CSS
cards.summary: When theme CSS is lazy-loaded, inline correct critical CSS so above-the-fold content is styled from the first paint and does not shift when the full stylesheet arrives.
cards.use_when: Your theme delays loading theme.css (or otherwise renders unstyled content briefly) and Lighthouse shows layout shift in the first second on home, collection or product templates.
steps: Confirm the pattern: theme.css downloads only after the rest of the DOM, so for the first second elements render unstyled and then jump into place when CSS loads — often invisible to the eye but captured by Google's test.
Add inline critical CSS for the visible portion of each template so the page looks correct before theme.css arrives.
In the source's example, the theme already had critical CSS for home, collection and product pages, but it was incomplete/miscompiled — the fix was recompiling a correct critical CSS file.
Compile critical CSS with an online critical-CSS generator: feed the full theme CSS file plus the URL you want critical CSS for.
Create separate critical CSS for visually different templates (e.g. a collection page with a banner vs one without).
Insert the snippet that serves the critical CSS inline in theme.liquid, then test repeatedly with Lighthouse, zooming out to catch below-the-fold shifts too.
For any element still moving (e.g. font-size changes), add a CSS rule reserving its final size so the change no longer displaces neighbors.
caveats: Does not fully fix below-the-fold elements; the source admits Google weighs those less but says fixing them anyway is worthwhile.
Lighthouse shows fewer issues than Google Speed Insights; address Lighthouse first, then move to Google's list.

cards.title: Reserve Space for Widgets That Inject Late
cards.summary: Eliminate layout shift from app widgets (review, Afterpay, etc.) by pinning a fixed container size in CSS for the space the widget will occupy.
cards.use_when: A review app, payment widget or similar injected element visibly jumps into place and pushes other content during your store's load, on home, product or collection pages.
steps: Identify the injected widget by watching the Lighthouse original trace or reloading the page; note exactly which element appears and how far it pushes content.
Determine the size the widget needs (inspect it after it renders, or check the app's documentation) then add a CSS rule fixing its container's width and height.
If two CSS files conflict on the same element's height, remove one of the contradicting rules instead of stacking more overrides.
Re-test with Lighthouse and confirm the shift is gone, both at normal zoom and zoomed out to surface below-the-fold shifts the source admits are lower priority.
Cross-check in Google Speed Insights, which surfaces elements Lighthouse omits, and add CSS rules preventing those from shifting too.
caveats: Ongoing Google Speed Insights may show green while Search Console lags by a couple of days.
Presenter's position: most CLS he sees is a CSS issue or an app widget needing reserved space, but other causes exist.

cards.title: Defer or Lazy-Trigger App Scripts to Shield Core Assets
cards.summary: Move non-visible app scripts out of the initial load, then inject them on user interaction so they no longer block store rendering.
cards.use_when: Speed tests flag unused jQuery/app JavaScript that loads in the first second even though the app's widget is not visible, and you still need the app for later interaction (e.g. reviews, SMS).
steps: Screen every installed app against one question: does it directly impact conversion or user experience? If not, remove it; if yes, check whether it needs to load in the first second at all.
On scripts you control (from theme.liquid), add defer or async so they load after core assets; test the app afterwards, as some break with these properties.

For scripts injected by an app's async function, locate the injected script in the theme's head, copy its URL, modify content_for_header to exclude that URL, and list the modified content_for_header — this stops the automatic injection.
Then create a snippet (e.g. lazy-scripts.liquid) containing vanilla JS that re-creates the script tag with that src, triggered on a click or scroll event; render it from theme.liquid.
Re-run the speed test to confirm the delayed app still fires immediately when the user clicks or scrolls, and that the score improves.
caveats: Scripts with pixels/tracking important for ad campaigns (e.g. Facebook, Google) should stay in the initial load and not be deferred.
Delayed app loading is only safe when the widget is not needed above the fold; verify each app still functions.

cards.title: Assess Whether Each Blocking Script Is Visible or Pixels
cards.summary: Triage blocking JavaScript by asking whether the script needs to run in the first second, and cut or delay the ones that don't.
cards.use_when: Google speed tests flag unused JavaScript / 'reduce unused JavaScript' on your home, collection or product page and you need to decide which scripts to keep, defer or remove.
steps: Read the flagged items: 'unused JavaScript' usually means unused during the test's window, not permanently — decide if each script is needed right away.
Begin with an app inventory: remove apps that add no value, that are purely visual, or that you no longer use; uninstalling still leaves residual script tags you must search out and delete.

For each remaining script, check whether its widget is actually visible at load. The source's example: Yotpo and Recharge widgets exist only on collection/product pages, so they don't need to run on the home page.
Conditionally load app assets only on templates that use their widget; this also removes associated 'reduce unused CSS' warnings for that app.
Keep pixels (Facebook, Google) and measurement tools in the initial load since they must track the user right away; keep Hotjar for interaction measurement.
Investigate duplicate injections — e.g. a Facebook script added both manually in theme.liquid and via an app — and eliminate the duplicate.
caveats: You may not be able to minify app-provided code; instead cut it from pages where it isn't needed.
Some app assets (e.g. ones without compression) are outside your control unless you raise it with the app's support or drop the app.

cards.title: Clean Residual Scripts After Uninstalling Apps
cards.summary: Uninstalling an app leaves its scripts in theme.liquid, head.liquid and footer.liquid — remove each residual tag to reclaim speed.
cards.use_when: You have removed or no longer use an app (or plugin) but its assets may still be loading and slowing your Shopify store.
steps: Open theme.liquid and search for the app's name (the source's example searches for 'yotpo' after uninstalling the Yotpo reviews app) and delete every script tag containing it.
Do the same in head.liquid and footer.liquid, since injected assets may live in any of these theme files.
Also audit scripts and style tags for plugins you stopped using — they often linger and keep loading.
Review the full contents of theme.liquid, head.liquid and footer.liquid and judge each entry's relevance; remove any asset with no current function.
Re-run speed tests to confirm the residual assets are gone and the store loads without them.
caveats: Removing script tags can break an app you are still using — verify the specific app is truly uninstalled or unused first.

cards.title: Right-Size Images and Pick the Correct Format
cards.summary: Shrink product/hero images and choose JPEG/PNG/MP4 by need rather than uploading DSLR originals.
cards.use_when: Speed tests show images are too large for mobile, or your store's pages load slowly because of oversized image assets.
steps: Convert large source images to a full-HD-size JPEG compressed under 1 MB — the source states this is sufficient for any screen size, especially for mobile-majority traffic.
Use PNG only when the image needs a transparent background; avoid animated GIFs (unprofessional and heavy) and instead upload a compressed MP4 using an HTML video tag.
For above-the-fold assets like the first hero or main product image, do not lazy-load them; they should load immediately.
Use preload='none' on videos so they load without blocking other elements.
Apply loading='lazy' to images not initially visible; for a carousel, lazy-load the second, third (etc.) images but not the first.
caveats: 'Under 1 MB JPEG is sufficient for any screen' is the presenter's rule of thumb, not a measurement of your specific catalog.
Lazy-loading the first visible image causes layout issues and hurts speed — the source calls this out as a common mistake.

cards.title: Use lazy-sizes for Bulletproof Image Lazy Loading
cards.summary: Trade the SRC for an empty pixel plus a data-src and lazy-load class, then let lazy-sizes swap in the real image.
cards.use_when: You want stronger lazy loading than the native loading='lazy' attribute gives, e.g. for a slide-out drawer or list of images below the fold.
steps: Install a lazy loading plugin like lazy-sizes on your theme.
On each image to lazy-load, set src to an empty pixel, add data-src with the real image URL, and add the plugin's lazy-load class.
Let lazy-sizes replace the src with the data-src URL once the image is needed, so the DOM downloads without being blocked by image requests.
Verify behavior: in the source's example, the drawer's images show gray placeholders first, then the real files download.
Never apply this to images in the initial viewport (hero, first carousel image, main product image).
caveats: The presenter's opinion is that lazy-sizes does the job slightly better than the native property, but the native property works.
Adding it to an image already visible at load defeats the purpose and creates the very layout issues you're avoiding.

cards.title: Font Loading: Add font-display: swap
cards.summary: Large custom font files block text rendering — font-display: swap lets a default font show immediately.
cards.use_when: Your theme uses multiple custom fonts and speed tests show text-rendering delays or layout shifts caused by font loading.
steps: Locate the @font-face rules in your theme's CSS files.
Add font-display: swap to each @font-face rule that lacks it, so a default font displays while the custom font downloads.
This prevents text from being blocked and reduces perceived load time and shift from font-size changes.
If a font-size change still shifts layout, add a CSS rule reserving the element's final size so neighbors don't move.
caveats: Multiple custom fonts increase asset size; consolidating font files reduces the problem at the source.

cards.title: Defer and Async Scripts to Prioritize Core Assets
cards.summary: Add defer/async to non-critical scripts so hero images and core assets download first.
cards.use_when: You control script tags in theme.liquid and want app/plugin scripts to stop delaying core asset loading.
steps: List the scripts in theme.liquid and ask, for each: does this need to load before or after the site is fully loaded?
For scripts not needed immediately, add the defer attribute so they execute after core assets finish; add async to load them in parallel without blocking, when order doesn't matter.
Common candidates for deferral: app scripts whose widgets aren't above the fold; tracking pixels (e.g. Facebook, Google) are the exception that should stay immediate.
Test after altering each script — the source notes some apps stop working when defer or async is added.
Go a step further (for a developer) by loading the entire store and core assets with no app scripts, then injecting those scripts on a click or scroll event.
caveats: Some apps break with defer/async — verify functionality after each change.
The interaction-triggered injection approach may require a specialist to tailor to your scenario.

cards.title: Delay Non-Visible CSS with media-onload-Print
cards.summary: CSS for elements not visible at load can be applied after the page loads, reducing render-blocking time.
cards.use_when: Large CSS files reference elements below the fold and your store's CSS is blocking rendering.
steps: Identify CSS files that style elements not visible during initial page load.
Apply the media='print' onload='this.media=all' technique so the stylesheet is fetched but only applied to the real view after load.
Keep critical CSS (above-the-fold styles) in place so the visible view stays styled from the first paint.
Re-test the page to confirm the CSS no longer blocks loading and the visible area remains correct.
caveats: Confirm the delayed CSS genuinely styles only below-the-fold elements; misapplying it leaves visible content unstyled.

cards.title: Evaluate Speed-Apps and Optimization Vendors Skeptically
cards.summary: Speed optimization apps are not the answer and some vendors use tricks that help the score but not real users.
cards.use_when: You are considering buying a speed-optimization app or hiring a speed specialist for your Shopify store.
steps: Treat 'speed-up' apps with caution: the source states they only work with returning users, if at all.
When hiring a specialist, verify improvements with your own real-user-timing data, not just a Google score — the audience sees tricks that improve ratings while end-user load stays slow.
Accept that there is no fast, one-action fix; expect a series of small changes across pages and templates.

Prioritize serving what's needed for the current view first rather than loading the whole asset library in the first seconds — the source's restaurant analogy: serve the drink, appetizer, first course rather than cooking the entire menu at once.
Work through fixes template by template: after fixing the main page-type templates, also run and fix secondary product/collection templates.
caveats: The 'returning users only' claim is the presenter's experience, not a measured benchmark.

cards.title: Check Page Vitals Before Trusting Them
cards.summary: Passing vitals (LCP/CLS) does not guarantee a good speed score — validate all three key pages.
cards.use_when: Your home page shows 'all vitals passed' and you're deciding whether store speed is genuinely healthy, or you're auditing a store for the first time.
steps: Run speed tests on all three pages Shopify uses — home, a collection page and a product page — not just the home page.
Do not equate passed vitals with a good score; the source's example store passed vitals yet scored 18 on home, 38 on collection and worse on product, combining to roughly 20.
Aggregate a picture across pages: pages can carry different apps/scripts, so one page may be fine while another is broken.
Fix the main issues (app load, JS blocking, image sizing, CSS), then expect new issues to surface in the test list as old ones are cleared.
Re-run every page type and every unique template repeatedly until the score improves.
caveats: The 18/38/≈20 figures are one audited store's example, not benchmarks for your store.

cards.title: Reproduce the Original Page-Speed Audit Method
cards.summary: A repeatable pass: inventory apps, cut blocking JS, size images, fix CSS, and test home/collection/product pages.
cards.use_when: You're running a full speed audit of your own Shopify store for the first time and need a consistent sequence of steps.
steps: Install no new apps yet; first inventory existing apps and remove any that don't directly affect conversion or UX.
Look at the JavaScript blocking delay (the source's example showed 2.7s from apps) and check for duplicates like Facebook pixel loaded twice (e.g. manual edit plus app).

For each app script, ask whether it needs to load at page load: social widget, PostScript, etc. can often be loaded later or removed if unused. Keep pixels and heatmaps (Facebook, Google, Hotjar) since they must measure right away.
Fix image sizing flagged as too large for mobile, and apply lazy loading to below-the-fold images only — not the first hero, first carousel slide or product image.
Address blocking CSS — separate critical CSS from non-visible stylesheets — and fix any CSS delays from app widgets.
Where app assets lack compression or minification, either contact the app's support or remove the app; then re-test home, collection and product pages.
caveats: Some listed issues (app compression/minification) are outside your control if you keep the app.
The presenter notes more advanced fixes exist beyond this main list.
